The repeat() function repeats two style values three times, creating a list of eight style values. As there are fewer row gutters than total gap-rules, the last three values in the list are discarded. ### Using auto within repeat() This example demonstrates using the auto argument instead of an integer in the repeat() function. #### CSS Using repeat(auto, ), we set all row rules to 1px dotted and default to the current color, except the first and last, which we set to 3px solid red. css live-sample___auto ul { row-rule: 3px red solid, repeat(auto, 1px dotted), 3px red solid; } #### Result css hidden live-sample___basic live-sample___repeat live-sample___func live-sample___auto @layer no-support { @supports not (row-rule: thin, thick) { body::before { content: "Your browser doesn't support the row-rule property"; background-color: wheat; display: block; text-align: center; padding: 1rem 0; } } } ## Specifications ## Browser compatibility ## See also - - - - shorthand - shorthand - CSS gaps module

title: XRView: isFirstPersonObserver property
content: The interface's read-only **isFirstPersonObserver** property is a boolean indicating if the XRView is a first-person observer view. To create video recordings of AR device cameras, you can't simply use one of the rendered eyes, as there often will be a physical offset. Some devices expose a secondary view, the first-person observer view, which has an eye of none. To receive a first-person observer view, you need to enable the "secondary-views" feature descriptor explicitly (typically as an optional feature). See for details. The isFirstPersonObserver property then allows you to check which secondary view is a first-person observer view. ## Examples ### Checking for first-person observer views js // Make sure to enable "secondary-view" navigator.xr .requestSession("immersive-ar", { optionalFeatures: ["secondary-views"], }) .then((session) => { // … session.requestAnimationFrame((frame) => { const views = frame.getViewerPose(space); // Make sure to iterate over all views for (const view of views) { if (view.isFirstPersonObserver) { renderFPO(); } else { render(); } } }); }); ## Specifications ## Browser compatibility

title: `corner-right-shape` CSS property
content: The **corner-right-shape** CSS property specifies the shape of both the corners on a box's right-hand edge, within their area. For a full description of corner shape behavior and multiple examples, see the shorthand property page. ## Constituent properties This property is a shorthand for the following physical properties: - - ## Syntax css /* Single keyword value set for both corners */ corner-right-shape: bevel; corner-right-shape: notch; /* Single superellipse() value set for both corners */ corner-right-shape: superellipse(4); corner-right-shape: superellipse(-0.9); /* Top corner, bottom corner */ corner-right-shape: bevel notch; corner-right-shape: notch superellipse(-0.9); /* Global values */ corner-right-shape: inherit; corner-right-shape: initial; corner-right-shape: revert; corner-right-shape: revert-layer; corner-right-shape: unset; ### Values The corner-right-shape property is specified using one or two values: - If **one value** is used, it specifies the shape of **both right-hand corners**. - If **two values** are used, the first one specifies the shape of the **top-right** corner, and the second one specifies the shape of the **bottom-right** corner. ## Formal definition ## Formal syntax ## Examples You can find other related examples on the reference page. ### Basic corner-right-shape usage #### HTML The markup for this example contains a single element. html live-sample___basic-usage #### CSS We give the box some basic styles, which we've hidden for brevity. We also apply a , a border-radius of 20% 30% / 50% 40%, and a corner-right-shape of square scoop. css hidden live-sample___basic-usage body { font-family: "Helvetica", "Arial", sans-serif; width: 240px; margin: 20px auto; } div { width: 100%; height: 180px; display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; background-color: cyan; background-image: linear-gradient( to bottom, rgb(255 255 255 / 0), rgb(255 255 255 / 0.5) ); } css live-sample___basic-usage div { box-shadow: 1px 1px 3px gray; border-radius: 20% 30% / 50% 40%; corner-right-shape: square scoop; } #### Result The rendered result looks like this: ## Specifications ## Browser compatibility ## See also - shorthand property - , , and - , , , and - shorthand property - and - CSS borders and box decorations module - CSS backgrounds and borders module

title: `baseline-source` CSS property
content: The **baseline-source** CSS property defines which baseline to use when inline-level boxes have multiple possible baselines, such as multi-line inline blocks or inline flex containers. The values allow for choosing between aligning to the box's first baseline, last baseline, or letting the browser decide automatically based on the box type. ## Syntax css /* Keyword values */ baseline-source: auto; baseline-source: first; baseline-source: last; /* Global values */ baseline-source: inherit; baseline-source: initial; baseline-source: revert; baseline-source: revert-layer; baseline-source: unset; ### Values - auto - : Specifies last baseline alignment for inline-block, first baseline alignment for everything else. - first - : Specifies first baseline alignment. - last - : Specifies last baseline alignment. ## Formal definition ## Formal syntax ## Examples ### Baseline selection in inline flex containers This example demonstrates using the baseline-source property to control the baseline alignment of inline flex containers. #### HTML Our HTML includes several elements, which are generic inline containers for phrasing content. Three of the elements contain nested children. html Baseline ___ First A B C Auto A B C A B C Last #### CSS css hidden body { font-family: sans-serif; } .box { border: 2px solid #888888; width: 50px; } span { padding: 0.4rem; } We define all the boxes to be inline flex containers. We set the .first box to use the first baseline, the .auto box uses the default baseline (which is first for inline flex containers), and the .last box uses the last baseline. css .box { display: inline-flex; flex-direction: column; } .first { baseline-source: first; } .auto { baseline-source: auto; } .last { baseline-source: last; } #### Result ## Specifications ## Browser compatibility ## See also - property - CSS box alignment overview

title: for await...of
content: The **for await...of** statement creates a loop iterating over async iterable objects as well as sync iterables. This statement can only be used in contexts where await can be used, which includes inside an async function body and in a module. js interactive-example async function* foo() { yield 1; yield 2; } (async () => { for await (const num of foo()) { console.log(num); // Expected output: 1 break; // Closes iterator, triggers return } })(); ## Syntax js-nolint for await (variable of iterable) statement - variable - : Receives a value from the sequence on each iteration. May be either a declaration with const, let, or var, or an assignment target (e.g., a previously declared variable, an object property, or a destructuring pattern). Variables declared with var are not local to the loop, i.e., they are in the same scope the for await...of loop is in. - iterable - : An async iterable or sync iterable. The source of the sequence of values on which the loop operates. - statement - : A statement to be executed on every iteration. May reference variable. You can use a block statement to execute multiple statements. ## Description When a for await...of loop iterates over an iterable, it first gets the iterable's [Symbol.asyncIterator](/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Symbol/asyncIterator) method and calls it, which returns an async iterator. If the @asyncIterator method does not exist, it then looks for a [Symbol.iterator](/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Symbol/iterator) method, which returns a sync iterator. The sync iterator returned is then wrapped into an async iterator by wrapping every object returned from the next(), return(), and throw() methods into a resolved or rejected promise, with the value property resolved if it's also a promise. The loop then repeatedly calls the final async iterator's next() method and awaits the returned promise, producing the sequence of values to be assigned to variable. A for await...of loop exits when the iterator has completed (the awaited next() result is an object with done: true). Like other looping statements, you can use control flow statements inside statement: - stops statement execution and goes to the first statement after the loop. - stops statement execution and goes to the next iteration of the loop. If the for await...of loop exited early (e.g., a break statement is encountered or an error is thrown), the return() method of the iterator is called to perform any cleanup. The returned promise is awaited before the loop exits. for await...of generally functions the same as the for...of loop and shares many of the same syntax and semantics. There are a few differences: - for await...of works on both sync and async iterables, while for...of only works on sync iterables. - for await...of can only be used in contexts where await can be used, which includes inside an async function body and in a module. Even when the iterable is sync, the loop still awaits the return value for every iteration, leading to slower execution due to repeated promise unwrapping. - If the iterable is a sync iterable that yields promises, for await...of would produce a sequence of resolved values, while for...of would produce a sequence of promises. - For for await...of, the variable can be the identifier async (e.g., for await (async of foo)); for...of forbids this case. Like for...of, if you use a using declaration, then the variable cannot be called of: js-nolint example-bad for await (using of of []); // SyntaxError This is to avoid syntax ambiguity with the valid code for await (using of []), before using was introduced. ## Examples ### Iterating over async iterables You can also iterate over an object that explicitly implements async iterable protocol: js const LIMIT = 3; const asyncIterable = { Symbol.asyncIterator { let i = 0; return { next() { const done = i === LIMIT; const value = done ? undefined : i++; return Promise.resolve({ value, done }); }, return() { // This will be reached if the consumer called 'break' or 'return' early in the loop. return { done: true }; }, }; }, }; (async () => { for await (const num of asyncIterable) { console.log(num); } })(); // 0 // 1 // 2 ### Iterating over async generators Since the return values of async generator functions conform to the async iterable protocol, they can be looped using for await...of. js async function* asyncGenerator() { let i = 0; while (i { for await (const num of asyncGenerator()) { console.log(num); } })(); // 0 // 1 // 2 For a more concrete example of iterating over an async generator using for await...of, consider iterating over data from an API. This example first creates an async iterable for a stream of data, then uses it to find the size of the response from the API. js async function* streamAsyncIterable(stream) { const reader = stream.getReader(); try { while (true) { const { done, value } = await reader.read(); if (done) return; yield value; } } finally { reader.releaseLock(); } } // Fetches data from URL and calculates response size using the async generator. async function getResponseSize(url) { const response = await fetch(url); // Will hold the size of the response, in bytes. let responseSize = 0; // The for-await-of loop. Async iterates over each portion of the response. for await (const chunk of streamAsyncIterable(response.body)) { // Incrementing the total response length. responseSize += chunk.length; } console.log(Response Size: ${responseSize} bytes); // "Response Size: 1071472" return responseSize; } getResponseSize("https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/photos"); ### Iterating over sync iterables and generators for await...of loop also consumes sync iterables and generators. In that case it internally awaits emitted values before assign them to the loop control variable. js function* generator() { yield 0; yield 1; yield Promise.resolve(2); yield Promise.resolve(3); yield 4; } (async () => { for await (const num of generator()) { console.log(num); } })(); // 0 // 1 // 2 // 3 // 4 // compare with for-of loop: for (const numOrPromise of generator()) { console.log(numOrPromise); } // 0 // 1 // Promise { 2 } // Promise { 3 } // 4 If a sync generator yields a rejected promise, for await...of calls the generator's return() method before throwing the rejection reason, allowing finally blocks within that generator to run. js function* generatorWithRejectedPromises() { try { yield 0; yield 1; yield Promise.resolve(2); yield Promise.reject(new Error("failed")); yield 4; throw new Error("throws"); } finally { console.log("called finally"); } } (async () => { try { for await (const num of generatorWithRejectedPromises()) { console.log(num); } } catch (e) { console.log("caught", e); } })(); // 0 // 1 // 2 // called finally // caught Error: failed ## Specifications ## Browser compatibility ## See also - -

title: Sticky activation
content: **Sticky activation** (or "sticky user activation") is a window state that indicates a user has meaningfully and directly interacted with the window since page load. Once active, the state lasts for the duration of the session. The state is enabled following any user interaction, when the window has focus, that results in the browser generating one or more of the following: - A mousedown or pointerdown event for a mouse. - A pointerup event for any other kind of pointer. - A touchend event. - A keydown event, other than for the escape or browser shortcut keys. The window is not user-activated by events that aren't necessarily caused by intentional interaction with the window, such as mouse move events or wheel events. Sticky activation is used to control access to certain features, blocking them if the user hasn't interacted with the page. For example, it can be used to ensure that controlled features in cross-origin frames don't run code on page load. See Features gated by user activation for more information. The property can be used to programmatically check the current window's sticky activation state. ## See also - Comparison between transient and sticky activation in _Features gated by user activation_ - Related glossary terms: - - - HTML Living Standard > Sticky activation

title: ReportingObserver: disconnect() method
content: The **disconnect()** method of the interface stops a reporting observer that had previously started observing from collecting reports. After calling disconnect(), neither nor the reports parameter of the ReportingObserver() callback will return any reports. The associated observer will no longer be active. ## Syntax js-nolint disconnect() ### Parameters None. ### Return value None ( ). ## Examples ### Basic usage js const options = { types: ["deprecation"], buffered: true, }; const observer = new ReportingObserver((reports, observer) => { reportBtn.onclick = () => displayReports(reports); }, options); observer.observe(); // … observer.disconnect(); ## Specifications ## Browser compatibility ## See also - Reporting API

title: AsyncDisposableStack.prototype.move()
content: The **move()** method of instances creates a new AsyncDisposableStack instance that contains the same disposers as this stack, and then marks this stack as disposed, without calling any disposers. ## Syntax js-nolint move() ### Parameters None. ### Return value A new instance. ### Exceptions - - : Thrown if the stack is already disposed. ## Examples ### Claiming ownership of a stack js async function consumeStack(stack) { await using newStack = stack.move(); // newStack now owns the disposers console.log(stack.disposed); // true console.log(newStack.disposed); // false // newStack is disposed here immediately before the function exits } const stack = new AsyncDisposableStack(); console.log(stack.disposed); // false await consumeStack(stack); console.log(stack.disposed); // true ### Allowing resources to be disposed within two code paths The major use case of move() is when you have one or more resources which could either be disposed right here or could be persisted for later use. In this case, you can put the resources in an AsyncDisposableStack and then call move() when you need to persist the resources for later usage. js class PluginHost { #disposed = false; #disposables; #channel; #socket; static async init() { // Create an AsyncDisposableStack that is disposed when init exits. // If construction succeeds, we move everything out of stack and into // #disposables to be disposed later. await using stack = new AsyncDisposableStack(); const channel = stack.use(await getChannel()); const socket = stack.use(await getSocket()); // If we made it here, then there were no errors during construction and // we can safely move the disposables out of stack. return new PluginHost(channel, socket, stack.move()); // If construction failed, then stack would be disposed before reaching // the line above, which would dispose channel and socket in turn. } constructor(channel, socket, disposables) { this.#channel = channel; this.#socket = socket; this.#disposables = disposables; } async Symbol.asyncDispose { if (this.#disposed) { return; } this.#disposed = true; // Put this.#disposables into a using variable, so it is automatically // disposed when the function exits. await using disposables = this.#disposables; // NOTE: we can free #socket and #channel here since they will be // disposed by the call to disposablesSymbol.asyncDispose, below. // This isn't strictly a requirement for every disposable, but is // good housekeeping since these objects will no longer be useable. this.#socket = undefined; this.#channel = undefined; this.#disposables = undefined; } } ## Specifications ## Browser compatibility ## See also - Polyfill of AsyncDisposableStack.prototype.move in core-js - JavaScript resource management - -

title: SyntaxError: "use strict" not allowed in function with non-simple parameters
content: The JavaScript exception ""use strict" not allowed in function" occurs when a "use strict" directive is used at the top of a function with , , or . ## Message plain SyntaxError: Illegal 'use strict' directive in function with non-simple parameter list (V8-based) SyntaxError: "use strict" not allowed in function with default parameter (Firefox) SyntaxError: "use strict" not allowed in function with rest parameter (Firefox) SyntaxError: "use strict" not allowed in function with destructuring parameter (Firefox) SyntaxError: 'use strict' directive not allowed inside a function with a non-simple parameter list. (Safari) ## Error type . ## What went wrong? A "use strict" directive is written at the top of a function that has one of the following parameters: - - - A "use strict" directive is not allowed at the top of such functions per the ECMAScript specification. ## Examples ### Function statement In this case, the function sum has default parameters a=1 and b=2: js-nolint example-bad function sum(a = 1, b = 2) { // SyntaxError: "use strict" not allowed in function with default parameter "use strict"; return a + b; } If the function should be in strict mode, and the entire script or enclosing function is also okay to be in strict mode, you can move the "use strict" directive outside of the function: js example-good "use strict"; function sum(a = 1, b = 2) { return a + b; } ### Function expression A function expression can use yet another workaround: js-nolint example-bad const sum = function sum([a, b]) { // SyntaxError: "use strict" not allowed in function with destructuring parameter "use strict"; return a + b; }; This can be converted to the following expression: js example-good const sum = (function () { "use strict"; return function sum([a, b]) { return a + b; }; })(); ### Arrow function If an arrow function needs to access the this variable, you can use the arrow function as the enclosing function: js-nolint example-bad const callback = (...args) => { // SyntaxError: "use strict" not allowed in function with rest parameter "use strict"; return this.run(args); }; This can be converted to the following expression: js example-good const callback = (() => { "use strict"; return (...args) => this.run(args); })(); ## See also - - - - - -

title: `<video>` HTML video embed element
content: The ** ** HTML element embeds a media player which supports video playback into the document. You can use for audio content as well, but the element may provide a more appropriate user experience. html interactive-example Download the WEBM or MP4 video. The above example shows how to use the element. Similar to the element, we include a path to the media we want to display inside the src attribute; we can include other attributes to specify information such as video width and height, whether we want it to autoplay and loop, or to show the browser's default video controls, and so on. The content inside the opening and closing tags is shown as a fallback in browsers that don't support the element. ## Attributes Like all other HTML elements, this element supports the global attributes. - autoplay - : A Boolean attribute; if specified, the video automatically begins to play back as soon as it can without stopping to finish loading the data. > [!NOTE] > Modern browsers block audio (or videos with an unmuted audio track) from autoplaying, as sites that automatically play audio can be an unpleasant experience for users. See our autoplay guide for additional information about how to properly use autoplay. To disable video autoplay, autoplay="false" will not work; the video will autoplay if the attribute is there in the tag at all. To remove autoplay, the attribute needs to be removed altogether. > [!NOTE] > Videos with the loading="lazy" attribute set will not start downloading and autoplaying until the element is near or within the viewport. - controls - : If this attribute is present, the browser will offer controls to allow the user to control video playback, including volume, seeking, and pause/resume playback. - controlslist - : The controlslist attribute, when specified, helps the browser select what controls to show for the video element whenever the browser shows its own set of controls (that is, when the controls attribute is specified). The allowed values are nodownload, nofullscreen and noremoteplayback. Use the disablepictureinpicture attribute if you want to disable the Picture-In-Picture mode (and the control). - crossorigin - : This enumerated attribute indicates whether to use CORS to fetch the related video. CORS-enabled resources can be reused in the element without being _tainted_. The allowed values are: - anonymous - : Sends a cross-origin request without a credential. In other words, it sends the Origin: HTTP header without a cookie, X.509 certificate, or performing HTTP Basic authentication. If the server does not give credentials to the origin site (by not setting the Access-Control-Allow-Origin: HTTP header), the resource will be _tainted_, and its usage restricted. - use-credentials - : Sends a cross-origin request with a credential. In other words, it sends the Origin: HTTP header with a cookie, a certificate, or performing HTTP Basic authentication. If the server does not give credentials to the origin site (through Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: HTTP header), the resource will be _tainted_ and its usage restricted. When not present, the resource is fetched without a CORS request (i.e., without sending the Origin: HTTP header), preventing its non-tainted use in elements. If invalid, it is handled as if the enumerated keyword anonymous was used. See CORS settings attributes for additional information. - disablepictureinpicture - : Prevents the browser from suggesting a Picture-in-Picture context menu or to request Picture-in-Picture automatically in some cases. - disableremoteplayback - : A Boolean attribute used to disable the capability of remote playback in devices that are attached using wired (HDMI, DVI, etc.) and wireless technologies (Miracast, Chromecast, DLNA, AirPlay, etc.). In Safari, you can use x-webkit-airplay="deny" as a fallback. - height - : The height of the video's display area, in CSS pixels (absolute values only; no percentages). - loading - : Indicates how the browser should load the video (including any poster image): - eager - : Loads the video immediately, regardless of whether or not the video is currently within the visible viewport (this is the default value). - lazy - : Defers loading the video until it reaches a calculated distance from the viewport, as defined by the browser. Lazy loading avoids the network and storage bandwidth required to handle the video until it's reasonably certain that it will be needed. This improves the performance in most typical use cases. While explicit width and height attributes are recommended for all videos to avoid layout shift, they are especially important for lazy-loaded ones. Lazy-loaded videos will never be loaded if they do not intersect a visible part of an element, even if loading them would change that, because unloaded videos have a width and height of 0. It creates an even more disruptive user experience when the content visible in the viewport reflows in the middle of reading it. Lazy-loaded videos located in the visual viewport may not yet be visible when the Window event is fired. This is because the event is fired based on eager-loaded videos — lazy-loaded videos are not considered even if they are located within the visual viewport upon initial page load. Loading is only deferred when JavaScript is enabled. This is an anti-tracking measure, because if a user agent supported lazy loading when scripting is disabled, it would still be possible for a site to track a user's approximate scroll position throughout a session, by strategically placing videos in a page's markup such that a server can track how many videos are requested and when. > [!NOTE] > The loading="lazy" attribute also impacts the autoplay, poster, and preload attributes, as described in each of those sections of the page. - loop - : A Boolean attribute; if specified, the browser will automatically seek back to the start upon reaching the end of the video. - muted - : A Boolean attribute that indicates the default audio mute setting contained in the video. If set, the audio will be initially silenced. Its default value is false, meaning the audio will be heard when the video is played. > [!NOTE] > To unmute, setting muted="false" will not work; the audio will be muted if the attribute is present at all. To unmute, the attribute must be removed entirely. - playsinline - : A Boolean attribute indicating that the video is to be played "inline", that is, within the element's playback area. Note that the absence of this attribute _does not_ imply that the video will always be played in fullscreen. - poster - : A URL for an image to be shown while the video is downloading. If this attribute isn't specified, nothing is displayed until the first frame is available, then the first frame is shown as the poster frame. > [!NOTE] > Videos with the loading="lazy" attribute set will only download the poster resource once the video is near or within the viewport. - preload - : This attribute is intended to provide a hint to the browser about what the author thinks will lead to the best user experience regarding what content is loaded before the video is played. It may have one of the following values: - none: Indicates that the video should not be preloaded. - metadata: Indicates that only video metadata (e.g., length) is fetched. - auto: Indicates that the whole video file can be downloaded, even if the user is not expected to use it. - _empty string_: A synonym of the auto value. The default value is different for each browser. The spec advises it to be set to metadata. > [!NOTE] > > - Videos with the loading="lazy" attribute set will only apply the preload behavior once the video is near or within the viewport. > - The autoplay attribute has precedence over preload. If autoplay is specified, the browser would obviously need to start downloading the video for playback. > - The specification does not force the browser to follow the value of this attribute; it is a mere hint. - src - : The URL of the video to embed. This is optional; you may instead use the element within the video block to specify the video to embed. - width - : The width of the video's display area, in CSS pixels (absolute values only; no percentages). ## Events - - : The input buffer of a is ready to be processed. - - : The browser can play the media, but estimates that not enough data has been loaded to play the media up to its end without having to stop for further buffering of content. - - : The browser estimates it can play the media up to its end without stopping for content buffering. - - : The rendering of an is terminated. - - : The duration attribute has been updated. - - : The media has become empty; for example, this event is sent if the media has already been loaded (or partially loaded), and the load() method is called to reload it. - - : Playback has stopped because the end of the media was reached. - - : An error occurred while fetching the media data, or the type of the resource is not a supported media format. - - : The first frame of the media has finished loading. - - : The metadata has been loaded. - - : Fired when the browser has started to load the resource. - - : Playback has been paused. - - : Playback has begun. - - : Playback is ready to start after having been paused or delayed due to lack of data. - - : Fired periodically as the browser loads a resource. - - : The playback rate has changed. - - : A _seek_ operation completed. - - : A _seek_ operation began. - - : The user agent is trying to fetch media data, but data is unexpectedly not forthcoming. - - : Media data loading has been suspended. - - : The time indicated by the currentTime attribute has been updated. - - : The volume has changed. - - : Playback has stopped because of a temporary lack of data. ## Usage notes Browsers don't all support the same video formats; you can provide multiple sources inside nested elements, and the browser will then use the first one it understands. html Your browser doesn't support HTML video. Here is a link to the video instead. When using elements, the browser attempts to load each source sequentially. If a source fails (e.g., due to an invalid URL or unsupported format), the next source is attempted, and so on. An error event fires on the element after all sources have failed; error events are not fired on each individual element. We offer a substantive and thorough guide to media file types and the guide to the codecs supported for video. Also available is a guide to audio codecs that can be used with them. Other usage notes: - If you don't specify the controls attribute, the video won't include the browser's default controls; you can create your own custom controls using JavaScript and the API. See Creating a cross-browser video player for more details. - To allow precise control over your video (and audio) content, HTMLMediaElements fire many different events. In addition to providing controllability, these events let you monitor the progress of both download and playback of the media, as well as the playback state and position. - You can use the property to adjust the positioning of the video within the element's frame, and the property to control how the video's size is adjusted to fit within the frame. - To show subtitles/captions along with your video, you can use some JavaScript along with the element and the WebVTT format. See Adding captions and subtitles to HTML video for more information. - You can play audio files using a element. This can be useful if, for example, you need to perform audio with a WebVTT transcript, since the element doesn't allow captions using WebVTT. - To test the fallback content on browsers that support the element, you can replace with a non-existing element like . A good general source of information on using HTML is the HTML video and audio beginner's tutorial. ### Styling with CSS The element is a replaced element — its value is inline by default — but its default width and height in the viewport is defined by the video being embedded. There are no special considerations for styling ; a common strategy is to give it a display value of block to make it easier to position, size, etc., and then provide styling and layout information as required. Video player styling basics provides some useful styling techniques. ### Adding subtitles and other timed text tracks Timed text tracks for subtitles, closed captions, chapter headings, and so on, can be added declaratively by nesting the element. The tracks are specified in Web Video Text Tracks File Format (WebVTT) (.vtt files). For example, the HTML below includes the file "captions.vtt", which will be used to overlay closed captions on the video if captions are enabled by the user. html Timed text tracks can also be added programmatically using the WebVTT API. ### Detecting track addition and removal You can detect when tracks are added to and removed from a element using the and events. However, these events aren't sent directly to the element itself. Instead, they're sent to the track list object within the element's that corresponds to the type of track that was added to the element: - - : An containing all of the media element's audio tracks. Add a listener for addtrack to this object to be notified when new audio tracks are added to the element. - - : A containing all of the media element's video tracks. Add an addtrack listener to this object to be notified when video tracks are added to the element. - - : A containing all of the media element's text tracks (which are used for subtitles, closed captions, and so on). Add an addtrack listener to this object to be notified when text tracks are added to the element. For example, to detect when audio tracks are added to or removed from a element, you can use code like this: js const elem = document.querySelector("video"); elem.audioTracks.onaddtrack = (event) => { trackEditor.addTrack(event.track); }; elem.audioTracks.onremovetrack = (event) => { trackEditor.removeTrack(event.track); }; This code watches for audio tracks to be added to and removed from the element, and calls a hypothetical function on a track editor to register and remove the track from the editor's list of available tracks. You can also use to listen for the and events. ### Server support for video If the MIME type for the video is not set correctly on the server, the video may not show or show a gray box containing an X (if JavaScript is enabled). If you use Apache Web Server to serve WebM videos, you can fix this problem by adding the video file type extensions to the video/webm MIME type (the most common WebM file extension is .webm). To do this, edit the mime.types file in /etc/apache or use the AddType configuration directive in httpd.conf: plain AddType video/webm .webm Your web host may provide an easy interface to MIME type configuration changes for new technologies until a global update naturally occurs. ## Accessibility Videos should provide both captions and transcripts that accurately describe their content (see Adding captions and subtitles to HTML video for more information on how to implement these). Captions allow people who are experiencing hearing loss to understand a video's audio content as the video is being played, while transcripts allow people who need additional time to be able to review audio content at a pace and format that is comfortable for them. It's worth noting that while you can caption audio-only media, you can only do so when playing audio in a element since the video region of the element is used to present the captions. This is one of the special scenarios in which it's useful to play audio in a video element. If automatic captioning services are used, it is important to review the generated content to ensure it accurately represents the source video. In addition to spoken dialog, subtitles and transcripts should also identify music and sound effects that communicate important information. This includes emotion and tone: plain 14 00:03:14 --> 00:03:18 [Dramatic rock music] 15 00:03:19 --> 00:03:21 [whispering] What's that off in the distance? 16 00:03:22 --> 00:03:24 It's… it's a… 16 00:03:25 --> 00:03:32 [Loud thumping] [Dishes clattering] Captions should not obstruct the main subject of the video. They can be positioned using the align VTT cue setting. - Web Video Text Tracks Format (WebVTT) - WebAIM: Captions, Transcripts, and Audio Descriptions - MDN Understanding WCAG, Guideline 1.2 explanations - Understanding Success Criterion 1.2.1 | W3C Understanding WCAG 2.0 - Understanding Success Criterion 1.2.2 | W3C Understanding WCAG 2.0 ## Examples ### Single source This example plays a video when activated, providing the user with the browser's default video controls to control playback. #### HTML html Sorry, your browser doesn't support embedded videos, but don't worry, you can download it and watch it with your favorite video player! #### Result Until the video starts playing, the image provided in the poster attribute is displayed in its place. If the browser doesn't support video playback, it displays the fallback text. ### Multiple sources This example builds on the last one, offering three different sources for the media; this allows the video to be watched regardless of which video codecs are supported by the browser. #### HTML html Sorry, your browser doesn't support embedded videos, but don't worry, you can download the MP4 and watch it with your favorite video player! #### Result First AVI is tried. If that can't be played, MP4 is tried. A fallback message is displayed if the video element isn't supported, but not if all sources fail. Some media file types let you provide more specific information using the codecs parameter as part of the file's type string. For example, video/webm; codecs="vp8, vorbis" says that the file is a WebM video using VP8 for its video and Vorbis for audio. ## Technical summary Content categories Flow content , phrasing content, embedded content. If it has a controls attribute: interactive content and palpable content. Permitted content If the element has a src attribute: zero or more elements, followed by transparent content that contains no media elements–that is no or <video> . Else: zero or more elements, followed by zero or more elements, followed by transparent content that contains no media elements–that is no or <video> . Tag omission None, both the starting and ending tag are mandatory. Permitted parents Any element that accepts embedded content. Implicit ARIA role No corresponding role Permitted ARIA roles application DOM interface ## Specifications ## Browser compatibility ## See also - Guide to media types and formats on the web - Media container formats (file types) - Web video codec guide - Web audio codec guide - Positioning and sizing the picture within its frame: and - - HTML video and audio - Manipulating video using canvas - Configuring servers for Ogg media

title: HTMLInputElement: files property
content: The **HTMLInputElement.files** property allows you to access the selected with the element. ## Value A object listing the selected files, if any, or null if the **HTMLInputElement** is not of type="file". ## Examples The example below shows how you can access the **HTMLInputElement.files** property and log the name, date modified, size, and type of each file selected by the user. ### HTML html ### JavaScript Note that **HTMLInputElement.files** still returns an instance of even if no files are selected. Therefore it's safe to iterate through it with without checking if any files are selected. js const fileInput = document.getElementById("files"); console.log(fileInput.files instanceof FileList); // true even if empty for (const file of fileInput.files) { console.log(file.name); // prints file name let fileDate = new Date(file.lastModified); console.log(fileDate.toLocaleDateString()); // prints legible date console.log( file.size < 1000 ? file.size : ${Math.round(file.size / 1000)}KB, ); console.log(file.type); // prints MIME type } ## Specifications ## Browser compatibility ## See also -

title: `<input type="reset">` HTML attribute value
content: elements of type **reset** are rendered as buttons, with a default event handler that resets all inputs in the form to their initial values. html interactive-example Comments: css interactive-example .controls { padding-top: 1rem; display: grid; grid-template-rows: repeat(2, auto); grid-template-columns: 1fr 2fr; gap: 0.7rem; } label { font-size: 0.8rem; justify-self: end; } input[type="reset"] { width: 5rem; justify-self: end; } input[type="reset"] { grid-column: 2; grid-row: 2; } ## Value An element's value attribute contains a string that is used as the button's label providing the button with an . Buttons such as reset don't have a value otherwise. ### Setting the value attribute html ### Omitting the value attribute If you don't specify a value, you get a button with the default label (typically "Reset," but this will vary depending on the ): html ## Using reset buttons buttons are used to reset forms. If you want to create a custom button and then customize the behavior using JavaScript, you need to use , or better still, a element. You should usually avoid including reset buttons in your forms. They're rarely useful, and are instead more likely to frustrate users who click them by mistake (often while trying to click the submit button). ### A basic reset button We'll begin by creating a basic reset button: html Type in some sample text This renders like so: Try entering some text into the text field, and then pressing the reset button. ### Adding a reset keyboard shortcut To add a keyboard shortcut to a reset button — just as you would with any for which it makes sense — you use the accesskey global attribute. In this example, r is specified as the access key (you'll need to press r plus the particular modifier keys for your browser/OS combination; see accesskey for a useful list of those). html Type in some sample text The problem with the above example is that there's no way for the user to know what the access key is! This is especially true since the modifiers are typically non-standard to avoid conflicts. When building a site, be sure to provide this information in a way that doesn't interfere with the site design (for example by providing an easily accessible link that points to information on what the site access keys are). Adding a tooltip to the button (using the title attribute) can also help, although it's not a complete solution for accessibility purposes. ### Disabling and enabling a reset button To disable a reset button, specify the disabled attribute on it, like so: html You can enable and disable buttons at run time by setting disabled to true or false; in JavaScript this looks like btn.disabled = true or btn.disabled = false. > [!NOTE] > See the page for more ideas about enabling and disabling buttons. ## Validation Buttons don't participate in constraint validation; they have no real value to be constrained. ## Examples We've included basic examples above. There isn't really anything more to say about reset buttons. ## Technical summary Value A string used as the button's label Events Supported common attributes type and value IDL attributes value DOM interface Implicit ARIA Role button ## Specifications ## Browser compatibility ## See also - and the interface which implements it. - Forms and buttons - HTML forms - The element

title: Refresh header
content: The HTTP **Refresh** directs a web browser to either refresh or redirect the page when a specified amount of time has passed after the page was fully loaded. It is exactly equivalent to using in HTML. > [!NOTE] > Even though it's present in the HTTP response, the Refresh header is still handled by the HTML loading machinery and happens after HTTP or JavaScript redirects. See redirection order of precedence for more information. > [!NOTE] > When a refresh redirects to a new page, the header is included in the request for the new page (if permitted by the ), and is set to the referrer URL after navigating. Header type ## Syntax http Refresh: Refresh: , url= Refresh: ; url= - - : A non-negative number of seconds after which to refresh the page. Fractional parts are recognized but ignored; you should only specify integers. - - : If present, the browser will redirect to the specified URL instead of refreshing with the current URL. This URL can be quoted or unquoted. The url= prefix is case-insensitive and optional. ## Examples ### Refreshing a page after a specific time This header will cause the browser to refresh the page 5 seconds after it is fully loaded (that is, after the event): http Refresh: 5 ### Redirecting after a specific time This header will cause the browser to redirect to a URL 5 seconds after the page is fully loaded: http Refresh: 5; url=https://example.com/ > [!NOTE] > See the http-equiv="refresh" attribute in the HTML reference for important information about accessibility implications of automatic redirects. ## Specifications ## Browser compatibility ## See also - - Redirections in HTTP - The Refresh header is still with us HTTP Working Group message (2019)

title: Agent communication and coordination
content: **Agents** is the JavaScript formal terminology for describing autonomous JavaScript executors. Most JavaScript you write gets executed in a single thread, but you may create more threads with specific platform APIs such as web workers. This guide explains general computer science concepts related to thread coordination and how JavaScript implements them. It also introduces the APIs for enabling cross-thread communication: , , and . It is recommended to understand Typed arrays before reading this. Afterwards, you can continue with the Execution model reference to dive into the technical details. > [!NOTE] > In this article, we will use "thread" and "agent" interchangeably. An agent is a JavaScript engine abstraction, while a thread is an implementation detail; an agent may or may not run in a separate operating system thread. Technically, we should have used "agents" everywhere because you can only interact with agents in JavaScript, but when talking about general computer science concepts like locks, it's much more natural to use "threads". > > Also, this guide has nothing to do with AI agents. ## Communication between two agents The JavaScript language spec does not provide APIs for creating agents, getting a reference to another agent, or exchanging data between them. Although the concept of "workers" exists in both the web and in Node.js, their APIs are largely distinct. This guide uses web workers. ### Creating agents A parent agent creates and holds a reference to a child agent using the constructor: js // -- main.js -- const worker = new Worker("./worker.js", { type: "module" }); The parent agent can be a window or another worker. For example, to run this example in a browser, you can reference main.js in an HTML file: html ### Communication via messages Two agents communicate using _messages_. Messages are sent over _message channels_. The parent agent (main.js here) and its child agent (worker.js here) have a message channel by default, which routes to their default ports: - main.js sends messages using , and receives messages using the event on the worker object. - worker.js sends messages using , and receives messages using the event on self. However, this is limited to communication between the creator and the agent it creates. When you want any two agents to communicate, you need to use a dedicated . You pass one of its objects to the worker over the default channel, and then exclusively use that port: js // -- main.js -- const worker = new Worker("./worker.js", { type: "module" }); const { port1, port2 } = new MessageChannel(); // We'll explain the [port2] parameter soon worker.postMessage({ hereIsYourPort: port2 }, [port2]); // Mark the port as ready for receiving messages port1.start(); js // -- worker.js -- // Use top-level await (only available inside modules) so code following it // only evaluates when the port is received const port = await new Promise((resolve, reject) => { self.addEventListener( "message", (e) => { const port = e.data.hereIsYourPort; if (!(port instanceof MessagePort)) { reject(new Error("I'm expecting a dedicated port")); return; } resolve(port); }, { once: true }, ); }); // Mark the port as ready for receiving messages port.start(); > [!NOTE] > In all subsequent examples, we'll assume that these lines exist at the top of main.js and worker.js. We won't repeat them. Now, each agent can call and listen for events on the MessagePort object. Using message channels, you can also connect two agents that aren't in a parent-child relationship, such as two workers created by the same thread: js const { port1, port2 } = new MessageChannel(); const worker1 = new Worker("./worker1.js", { type: "module" }); const worker2 = new Worker("./worker2.js", { type: "module" }); worker1.postMessage({ hereIsYourPort: port1 }, [port1]); worker2.postMessage({ hereIsYourPort: port2 }, [port2]); As a practical example, we implement a number-guessing game. main.js defines a secret number, and worker.js tries to guess it. Each time, main.js tells worker.js whether the guess is correct, too low, or too high, and the worker adjusts its guess. Here's how main.js can receive guesses from the worker using , and provide feedback using port1.postMessage(): js // -- main.js -- const secretNumber = 63; port1.addEventListener("message", (e) => { const workerGuess = e.data; console.log("Worker guessed:", workerGuess); if (workerGuess secretNumber) { port1.postMessage("Too high"); } else { port1.postMessage("Correct"); console.log("Worker successfully guessed the secret number!"); } }); And here's how the worker can submit guesses to main.js and adjust based on the feedback from it: js // -- worker.js -- let low = 0; let high = 100; let lastGuess = Math.floor((low + high) / 2); // First guess submitted immediately after initialization port.postMessage(lastGuess); port.addEventListener("message", (e) => { const feedback = e.data; if (feedback === "Correct") { console.log("Yay"); return; } if (feedback === "Too low") { low = lastGuess + 1; } else if (feedback === "Too high") { high = lastGuess - 1; } if (low > high) { throw new Error( "Sorry, the feedback from main.js is inconsistent and I suspect main is cheating", ); } lastGuess = Math.floor((low + high) / 2); port.postMessage(lastGuess); }); port.start(); If you run this in a browser, both the worker and the main thread will output to the same DevTools console, so you will see the output as: plain Worker guessed: 50 main.js Worker guessed: 75 main.js Worker guessed: 62 main.js Worker guessed: 68 main.js Worker guessed: 65 main.js Worker guessed: 63 main.js Worker successfully guessed the secret number! main.js Yay worker.js ### Sending messages by copying or transferring You can pass many kinds of JavaScript values to postMessage. In the number-guessing example, we pass numbers for guesses, strings for feedback, and objects for the MessagePort. By default, each agent has its own memory space, so when an object is sent from one heap to another, a copy of it is created in the target heap. The copy uses the structured clone algorithm, which only supports a fixed set of data types. When you attempt to copy an unsupported object, a is thrown. Copying an object allows the sender and the recipient to independently manipulate the object without affecting the other. The downside is that the object is re-constructed in the recipient's scope, which means: - It's not tethered to the original creator, so can't work (indeed, if you read the list of serializable objects, you can see that MessagePort is not listed here). - There are two copies of the same data, which increases memory usage. To solve these problems, instead of copying objects, you can pass them by _transferring_ instead. Transferring an object uses a slightly different algorithm for constructing it in the target realm, and marks it as _detached_ in the source realm. The source object still exists, but its transferred resource is now available through the new object in the target realm: To transfer an object, you still pass it (or other objects containing it) to postMessage(). The second parameter of postMessage() takes a list of objects inside the message that should be transferred instead of copied. This explains the following line in the number guessing game: js worker.postMessage({ hereIsYourPort: port2 }, [port2]); The whole object { hereIsYourPort: port2 } is copied as usual and can be used in both agents, though it isn't assigned to a variable in the sender, so it will be immediately dropped over there. The port2 resource is taken over by the new object in the worker agent, while the source instance is marked as detached. The effects of detachment depend on the object type, but generally operations either throw an error or do nothing. For a MessagePort, the original object loses its connection to the other port. Other than MessagePort, another widely-used transferable object is , which happens to be both copyable and transferable. When an ArrayBuffer is copied, the source and recipient each hold an independent copy, and mutations on one side do not affect the other. When an ArrayBuffer is transferred, it is again marked as _detached_. A detached array buffer still exists as an object, but no longer provides access to the underlying memory. This means that: - becomes 0 (in both the buffer and the associated typed array views). - Methods, such as and , throw a when invoked. The associated typed array views' methods also throw a TypeError. You can check whether an ArrayBuffer is detached via its property. In pure JavaScript, you can also transfer the ownership of memory from one ArrayBuffer to another using its or method. js const buffer1 = new ArrayBuffer(1024); console.log(buffer1.detached); // false console.log(buffer1.byteLength); // 1024 const buffer2 = buffer1.transfer(); console.log(buffer1.detached); // true console.log(buffer1.byteLength); // 0 console.log(buffer2.byteLength); // 1024 ## Sharing memory with SharedArrayBuffer Other than copying and transferring, there's a third model of data passing: _sharing_. In sharing, both sides hold an object that shares the underlying memory. Memory sharing is available only to the object. The sender and recipient still hold distinct instances of the SharedArrayBuffer object, but they represent pointers to the same memory span and mutations on one side are visible to the other side. ### Enabling shared memory Memory sharing isn't inherently risky; however, it allows implementing a high-precision clock (we won't go into the details here), which was revealed to enable Spectre attacks. In response to this, browsers restrict shared memory access to cross-origin isolated websites only. > [!NOTE] > If you are using Node.js for this tutorial (which means you had been adapting the previous examples to Node-specific APIs), you can ignore this section, because shared memory is available by default. If you are using a local HTTP server to experiment with these examples, you must make your website cross-origin isolated, for example by sending the following headers: http Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin After you do this, you can perform the following checks to confirm that shared memory is enabled: js console.log(window.crossOriginIsolated); // true console.log("SharedArrayBuffer" in window); // true Now you can share memory, but only within an agent cluster—you can't share memory with agents outside of its cluster, even when they have a message channel. A window and its dedicated worker are in the same cluster, so our examples will work fine. ### Using a shared buffer The SharedArrayBuffer (SAB) interface is mostly identical to ArrayBuffer. You can construct a SharedArrayBuffer, which allocates the specified number of bytes. js const sab = new SharedArrayBuffer(1024); You can read and write the memory contents by constructing a view, such as an . js const int8 = new Int8Array(sab); int8[0] = 63; You can create a slice of the SAB, which allocates a new shared memory span and copies its contents. js const sab2 = sab.slice(); // Entire sab is copied const int82 = new Int8Array(sab2); console.log(int82[0]); // 63 There are several differences between SharedArrayBuffer and ArrayBuffer (other than memory-sharing behavior, of course): - Resizable SABs can only be _grown_, while normal resizable buffers can both be grown and shrunk. - SABs cannot be transferred/detached. To create a resizable/growable SAB, pass the maxByteLength option specifying the maximum length it's allowed to grow to. Then, you can use grow(). js const sabResizable = new SharedArrayBuffer(1024, { maxByteLength: 2048 }); console.log(sabResizable.byteLength); // 1024 sabResizable.grow(2000); console.log(sabResizable.byteLength); // 2000 ### Posting SharedArrayBuffers SharedArrayBuffer objects are always shared when passed to postMessage() (as long as the security requirements are met); no extra options are necessary. Both sides can mutate this memory span and observe the other side's mutations. You can also pass a view of a SharedArrayBuffer directly—the view and the buffer object are both copied, but the underlying memory span is still shared. In the following examples, we'll share a buffer between main.js and worker.js together with the message port. Replace the line in main.js: js worker.postMessage({ hereIsYourPort: port2 }, [port2]); With: js const sab = new SharedArrayBuffer(1024); worker.postMessage({ hereIsYourPort: port2, andHereIsOurSAB: sab }, [port2]); And inside worker.js, replace the initial reception code with: js const { port, sab } = await new Promise((resolve, reject) => { self.addEventListener( "message", (e) => { const port = e.data.hereIsYourPort; if (!(port instanceof MessagePort)) { reject(new Error("I'm expecting a dedicated port")); return; } const sab = e.data.andHereIsOurSAB; if (!(sab instanceof SharedArrayBuffer)) { reject(new Error("I'm expecting a shared array buffer")); return; } resolve({ port, sab }); }, { once: true }, ); }); To verify that this setup works, try coordinating a short write-read exchange using a message. The worker immediately updates the SharedArrayBuffer and posts a message to the main thread. The main thread receives that message and reads the new value. We'll talk about more efficient communications later. js // -- main.js -- const int8 = new Int8Array(sab); port1.addEventListener("message", (e) => { console.log(int8[0]); // 63 }); js // -- worker.js -- const int8 = new Int8Array(sab); int8[0] = 63; port.postMessage("I've modified the memory. Please check"); ## Accessing shared memory with Atomics In the example above, we use a message to force the following order: 1. Worker writes to memory 2. Worker posts message 3. Main agent receives message and runs event listener 4. Main agent reads memory The problem with event-based coordination is that events are asynchronous: the time between steps 2 and 3 is dependent on the browser's event loop. In this case, you might as well pass values back and forth without relying on shared memory. The advantage of shared memory is exactly that you can (mostly) communicate synchronously, without yielding the job queue to other async tasks. In a single agent, the run-to-completion semantics ensure well-behaved effect ordering with respect to multiple synchronous jobs: js const promise = Promise.resolve(); let i = 0; promise.then(() => { i += 1; console.log(i); }); promise.then(() => { i += 1; console.log(i); }); Here, the overall order is always i += 1; console.log(i); i += 1; console.log(i); and never i += 1; i += 1; console.log(i); console.log(i);. There aren't such guarantees when the synchronous jobs belong to different agents. In the example below, the worker sends the main agent a started message and immediately starts incrementing the shared integer in a loop. Upon receipt of the message, the main agent runs the same loop at the same time. When the worker finishes, it sends a finished message, and the main agent logs the final value. js // -- main.js -- const i = new Int32Array(sab, 0, 1); port1.addEventListener("message", ({ data }) => { if (data === "started") { for (let n = 0; n [!NOTE] > If you want to go further and guarantee that both new values are observed, you need to make both agents wait before the Atomics.load() call, such as using a while (Atomics.load(a, 1) === 0); loop. Furthermore, atomic load/store operations establish a partial ordering for other _non-atomic_ read/write operations. Specifically, if agent A runs Atomics.store(), and then agent B reads the same value with Atomics.load(), then all non-atomic writes executed by A before the atomic store must also become observable to all non-atomic reads executed by B after the atomic load. This essentially create a "synchronization point" between two threads, much like a message event. For example: js // -- main.js -- a[0] = 63; // Set a "Ready" flag in a[1]; assume initially it's not 1. Atomics.store(a, 1, 1); js // -- worker.js -- // Spin until a[1] receives the "Ready" flag while (Atomics.load(a, 1) !== 1); console.log(a[0]); // 63 > [!NOTE] > Within a single agent, the worker.js code would definitely be a bug because it's not possible for a[1] to have changed in the loop if the loop is never updating the value. Many synchronous infinite loops only make sense with shared memory! > > In Waiting and notifying, we'll see how to make this code slightly more performant and less like a bug. The only possible order is the following: 1. main.js writes a[0] = 63. worker.js keeps spinning in the while loop because a[1] isn't the right value. 2. main.js stores a[1] as 1. 3. worker.js loads the new a[1] value and exits the while loop. 4. worker.js reads a[0] as 63. We have successfully established an ordering from 1 to 4 with the help of the store/load pair, so worker.js can observe the new value of a[0] written by main.js, despite not using atomic operations. ### Atomic updates The next set of operations directly replace several compound assignment operators. As we already demonstrated, the += operator is not atomic: other instructions may execute between the read and the write, causing the final write to not write the value you expect. To fix this, you can replace it with : js // -- main.js -- const i = new Int32Array(sab, 0, 1); port1.addEventListener("message", ({ data }) => { if (data === "started") { for (let n = 0; n [!NOTE] > Unlike the previously-introduced methods, wait(), waitAsync(), and notify() can only operate on Int32Array and BigInt64Array views. Here, the worker.js thread is halted if a[1] === 0. js // -- worker.js -- Atomics.wait(a, 1, 0); console.log(a[0]); It stays halted until another thread—in our case, main.js—notifies it: js // -- main.js -- a[0] = 63; Atomics.store(a, 1, 1); Atomics.notify(a, 1); Some important notes to call out: - Atomics.wait() also blocks the thread from executing other jobs. On the web, the main thread cannot be blocked, so calling Atomics.wait() throws an error there. - Atomics.wait() returns whenever it has been notified, regardless of whether a[1] has actually changed. - Other than checking the initial value, the memory index that store and wait operate on is entirely arbitrary: they do not care what that value actually represents. The index serves as the ID of the list of waiting agents. The initial flag check ensures that if the worker wait happens after notify is already called, the wait continues immediately instead of sleeping forever, so you should set and only set a[1] to 1 (representing "Ready" in our case) immediately before calling notify. You can also specify a timeout, after which the thread resumes despite not receiving a notification: js // -- worker.js -- const result = Atomics.wait(a, 1, 0, 100); // Wait about 100ms if (result === "timed-out") { // Decide what to do here: wait again? Throw an error? // Change to an asynchronous wait instead? } else { // result can be either "not-equal" - i.e., a[1] is already "Ready" // without waiting or "ok" - i.e., some other thread notified it console.log(a[0]); } The method provides the same functionality as wait(), but in the form of a promise, thus allowing other asynchronous jobs to proceed in the meantime. js // -- main.js -- const result = Atomics.waitAsync(a, 1, 0, 100); // Wait about 100ms if (!result.async) { // Already ready // (Note: because timeout is not 0, result.value is always "not-equal") console.log(a[0]); } else { const resultValue = await result.value; if (resultValue === "ok") { console.log(a[0]); } else { // resultValue is "timed-out" here; decide what to do } } You must carefully weigh the impacts of the three waiting mechanisms: - Busy waiting blocks the thread without yielding the CPU. When it finishes, the CPU can immediately resume without context switching, but while it's spinning, this core is occupied and cannot take other jobs (although the operating system may decide to schedule in some other thread if the current thread has used the CPU for too long). This is the fastest mechanism when you expect the wait to be very short, even shorter than the time taken by two context switches. - Synchronous Atomics.wait() blocks the thread but yields the CPU. The CPU core can take other threads and may need to context switch when this thread continues. This is the most efficient mechanism when you expect the wait to be longer than two context switches and it might be better to let other threads use the CPU in the meantime, but you prefer to keep the code synchronous. - Asynchronous Atomics.waitAsync() uses normal promise semantics: the code that waits for its completion comes back as another job in the agent, but other code in the same thread keeps executing. This is useful when the current thread has other jobs that are equally important and must proceed in the meantime, such as the main thread, which needs to render the page and respond to user interactions. ## Useful shared memory patterns Let's look at a few common techniques and concepts for ensuring the performance and correctness of multi-threading. A shared memory protocol needs to answer these questions: - Who may access each part of the memory? - Which operations must happen together without interleaving operations from other threads? - How does an agent know that data is ready to read or safe to overwrite? - How much work does the protocol require when an agent is working alone, and what happens when many agents compete for access? ### Locks and mutexes A _lock_, also called a _mutex_ (for "mutual exclusion"), is a mechanism that ensures that while a thread has access to a particular resource, no other thread can have access to the same resource. Each thread acquires the lock before accessing protected data and releases it afterwards. The code between acquisition and release is called a _critical section_. > [!NOTE] > A _futex_ is short for a "fast user-space mutex", but somewhat confusingly, it is not a mutex—it is a waiting mechanism that can be used to implement a mutex. In JavaScript, futexes are the only built-in waiting mechanism, provided by Atomics.wait()/Atomics.waitAsync() and Atomics.notify(); our mutex examples build upon this mechanism. A mutex is merely a protocol and does not physically prevent another thread from accessing the memory. As long as the protocol is upheld, different threads will never have overlapping critical sections, thus protecting a whole sequence of operations without making each individual read and write atomic. For example, create a buffer with space for a lock and a value. In our protocol, each participating agent will create an Int32Array view where the first element represents the lock (1 means unlocked, 0 means locked) and the second holds the protected data. js const sab = new SharedArrayBuffer(8); const shared = new Int32Array(sab); shared[0] = 1; Here's how one participating agent may implement that protocol. When an agent calls lock() to try to acquire the lock: - Atomics.compareExchange() is called, attempting to set the first element to 0 (locked), but only if it's currently 1 (available). - If that fails—i.e., when it's already 0 because another agent is holding the lock—Atomics.wait() puts the caller to sleep, provided the lock still contains 0 (the lock may have been released between compareExchange() and wait()). - The agent will only wake up when the agent currently holding the lock calls unlock(), which both resets the lock element to 1 and wakes the earliest waiting agent in the queue with Atomics.notify(). - After waking, the agent tries to acquire the lock again, but it may still fail if there's a newcomer (for example, if the releasing agent immediately calls lock() again) who got the lock first, in which case this agent goes back to sleep again due to the while() loop. - The loop only exits when lock acquisition succeeds. js function lock() { while (Atomics.compareExchange(shared, 0, 1, 0) !== 1) { Atomics.wait(shared, 0, 0); } } function unlock() { Atomics.store(shared, 0, 1); Atomics.notify(shared, 0, 1); } Here's how the lock-unlock pair can be called. The critical section must be wrapped in a block, with unlock() called in finally, so the lock is released even if the critical section throws an exception: js lock(); try { shared[1] *= 2; shared[1] += 1; } finally { unlock(); } Although the critical section uses ordinary indexed read/write, other agents will never observe stale values, because the atomic operations in lock()/unlock() establish a sequentially-consistent ordering. One mutex around all shared data is a straightforward starting point, but it serializes all protected work. If agents can operate on independent regions, giving those regions separate locks—or assigning each region to a single writer—can allow more concurrency. This simple mutex has multiple opportunities for improvement: - What if an agent accidentally calls unlock() when the lock wasn't actually held by it? - : We can solve this by replacing the boolean flag with a unique ID for each agent, so unlock() only proceeds if the ID in the lock matches the agent ID. - What if an agent accidentally calls lock() when it's already holding the lock (this is called _re-entry_)? This would cause it to wait on itself indefinitely, and all other agents waiting for the lock will also never get it. - : We can solve this by making lock() only wait if the owner ID in the lock doesn't match the current ID. > [!NOTE] > Re-entry is commonly seen in nested function calls; for example if a critical section calls another function that also tries to establish a critical section using the same lock. If the lock is non-reentrant (it doesn't implement this mechanism), then each agent must ensure that the critical section is never re-entered. - What if the agent that re-enters the lock calls unlock()? This would cause the lock to be released early, despite there being another lock() call that expects the lock to still be held. - : We need to add a counter that increments on each lock() and decrements on each unlock(), and only actually release the lock when the counter reaches zero. - What if the waiting agent always loses to a newcomer and never gets the lock? - : We need some scheduling mechanism to ensure that the newcomer doesn't jump the queue. ### Spinlocks In the example above, an agent waiting for the lock goes to sleep and requires the other agent to notify it with unlock(). This is efficient when contention is high, because the lock may not be acquired quickly and it's best to yield the CPU to other processes not needing the lock. But when contention is low, scheduling the thread in and out of the CPU creates extra overhead compared to just occupying the CPU while waiting. A _spinlock_ uses busy waiting instead of putting contenders to sleep. To turn the previous mutex into a spinlock, replace its functions with: js function lock() { while (Atomics.compareExchange(shared, 0, 1, 0) !== 1) { Atomics.pause(); } } function unlock() { Atomics.store(shared, 0, 1); } The Atomics.pause() here is just a performance hint to the CPU. You can remove it and still keep the same functionality. > [!WARNING] > Using spinlocking on the main thread is not recommended, as it will freeze the entire page. In general, unless designed very carefully, spinlocks may not actually be more performant than a regular wait. Sometimes, whether contention is high or low is not for you to decide while writing the code. The same code may run when there are only two contenders and busy-waiting is more efficient, or when there are a thousand contenders and it must use a regular wait. In this case, you can use a hybrid approach, which is to first spin for a little while (say, 10 iterations), and if the lock is still not acquired, then call Atomics.wait(). There's an example on the page. ### Semaphores A mutex only allows one agent to access the resource at a time; a _semaphore_, on the other hand, generalizes that to allow up to a specified number of simultaneous agents. To implement this, the shared memory maintains a count of available _permits_: acquiring a permit decrements the count, releasing one increments it, and an agent waits if no permits are available. js const sab = new SharedArrayBuffer(4); const permits = new Int32Array(sab); permits[0] = 3; Each worker creates its own view of that buffer and uses the following functions: js const permits = new Int32Array(sab); function acquire() { while (true) { const available = Atomics.load(permits, 0); if (available === 0) { Atomics.wait(permits, 0, 0); } else if ( Atomics.compareExchange(permits, 0, available, available - 1) === available ) { return; } } } function release() { Atomics.add(permits, 0, 1); Atomics.notify(permits, 0, 1); } acquire(); try { // Perform a task that requires one permit. } finally { release(); } You might notice that if we set the maximum number of permits to 1, we arrive at essentially the same code as the mutex example—indeed, our simple mutex is just a _binary semaphore_ (at most 1 permit). A semaphore with multiple permits (called a _counting semaphore_) still runs into problems when the concurrent agents try to access the same resource. The goal of a semaphore is to moderate access to a limited resource pool (for example, if there are only 4 available buffers). You still need a separate mechanism to assign these resources to the agents to avoid simultaneous access. ### Avoiding deadlocks A _deadlock_ occurs when agents wait on each other in a cycle, so none can make progress. For example: 1. Agent A acquires lock X. 2. Agent B acquires lock Y. 3. Agent A waits to acquire Y, while still holding X. 4. Agent B waits to acquire X, while still holding Y. js // -- a.js -- lockX.lock(); try { lockY.lock(); // Waiting for lockY.unlock() in b.js... try { // Work requiring both locks } finally { lockY.unlock(); } } finally { lockX.unlock(); } js // -- b.js -- lockY.lock(); try { lockX.lock(); // Waiting for lockX.unlock() in a.js... try { // Work requiring both locks } finally { lockX.unlock(); } } finally { lockY.unlock(); } Neither agent can reach the code that releases its lock. Waiting on a lock is just one way to enter a deadlock: two agents may also wait on a message from the other agent, etc. Preventing deadlocks requires very high discipline within each agent. For example, when an operation needs multiple locks, the protocol must specify the order in which these locks are acquired. Each agent must make sure that locks are eventually released, especially in case of errors (by using try...finally). How such protocols can be enforced at the compiler or static checker level is an active area of research. ### Lock-free algorithms Locks are powerful and convenient (when implemented correctly), but they are also a bit heavyweight, especially when there's no contention. For every critical section—which may be as short as a single read/write operation—the mutex above incurs the overhead of an Atomics.compareExchange(), an Atomics.store(), and—except when using spinlocks—an Atomics.notify(). In fact, even something as simple as Atomics.load(uint16, 0) might need an internal lock! If you think about it, an element in a Uint16Array is comprised of two bytes. If an extremely simple CPU only allows reading memory byte-by-byte, it would look like the following (assuming little-endian byte order): js const firstByte = uint8[0]; // uint8 is the same memory span viewed as Uint8Array const secondByte = uint8[1]; const value = firstByte + (secondByte { worker.addEventListener("message", resolve, { once: true }); }); while (true) { // Wait until the worker finishes its turn while (Atomics.load(shared, 0) !== 1) { // We use busy waiting here because we expect the worker to come // back very quickly and the main thread can't use Atomics.wait(). // In more complex scenarios, you probably want to use Atomics.waitAsync() // to avoid blocking the main thread. Atomics.pause(); } const workerGuess = shared[1]; console.log("Worker guessed:", workerGuess); const feedback = workerGuess secretNumber ? 1 : 0; shared[1] = feedback; Atomics.store(shared, 0, 0); Atomics.notify(shared, 0, 1); if (feedback === 0) { console.log("Worker successfully guessed the secret number!"); break; } } js // -- worker.js -- const sab = await new Promise((resolve) => { self.addEventListener("message", (e) => resolve(e.data), { once: true }); }); const shared = new Int32Array(sab); let low = 0; let high = 100; // Tell the main thread that the worker has started self.postMessage("ready"); while (true) { const lastGuess = Math.floor((low + high) / 2); // Worker initiates the handoff here by making a guess shared[1] = lastGuess; Atomics.store(shared, 0, 1); Atomics.notify(shared, 0, 1); // Wait until the main agent writes the feedback while (Atomics.load(shared, 0) !== 0) { Atomics.wait(shared, 0, 1); } const feedback = shared[1]; if (feedback === 0) { console.log("Yay"); break; } if (feedback === -1) { low = lastGuess + 1; } else if (feedback === 1) { high = lastGuess - 1; } if (low > high) { throw new Error( "Sorry, the feedback from main.js is inconsistent and I suspect main is cheating", ); } } This implements the same functionality, and note how both loops are synchronous—this should be much more efficient than passing messages back and forth! ## See also - JavaScript execution model - Web workers API - - -

title: Fundamental text and font styling
content: In this article we'll start you on your journey towards mastering text styling with . Here we'll go through all the basic fundamentals of text/font styling in detail, including setting font weight, family and style, font shorthand, text alignment and other effects, and line and letter spacing. Prerequisites: Structuring content with HTML and CSS Styling basics . Learning outcomes: Understanding the concepts of font families, font stacks, and web-safe fonts.
